1.2.3.14-f1.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.18.14–15 lists 'caecus Amor sui' with 'Gloria' among the companions of drunken excess, as the note says.

1.2.3.14-f108.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Aeneid 6.842–43 has 'duo fulmina belli, / Scipiadas'.

1.2.3.14-f11.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.39–40 is quoted correctly, and Burton's abridgement is described accurately.

1.2.3.14-f121.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, De grammaticis 23 says of Remmius Palaemon both that he called Varro a pig and that he boasted letters were born and would die with him.

1.2.3.14-f131.accuracy_reason: Pliny Ep. 5.8 to Titinius Capito reads 'si qua me quoque possim tollere humo', echoing Virgil, Georgics 3.8–9; the variant 'levare' is correctly reported.

1.2.3.14-f132.accuracy_reason: Correct: this is Metamorphoses 15.871–876, and Ovid's text has 'cum volet, illa dies'.

1.2.3.14-f19.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 14.34–35 applies this line to the few young men who resist their parents' bad example. Identifying Titan as Prometheus, maker of men from clay, is the standard reading.

1.2.3.14-f27.accuracy_reason: Rubbing books with cedar oil and storing them in cypress cases is correct. Horace, Ars Poetica 332, reads 'levi'.

1.2.3.14-f32.accuracy_reason: This is Ennius's epitaph on himself, quoted by Cicero (Tusculan Disputations 1.34). The usual text is 'volito vivus per ora virum'.

1.2.3.14-f36.accuracy_reason: The story of Phryne offering to rebuild the walls of Thebes if her name were inscribed on them is told in Athenaeus 13.591d. Burton's 'Phryne fecit' is a short form of the inscription she wanted.

1.2.3.14-f39.accuracy_reason: Correct: the proverb 'sexagenarios de ponte' (Festus; Erasmus, Adagia) refers to men over sixty being kept off the voting gangway.

1.2.3.14-f45.accuracy_reason: Martial 5.52 is about favours spoiled when the giver keeps talking about them. The line reads 'auctoris pereunt garrulitate sui'.

1.2.3.14-f47.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 2.1.60–61, Trebatius warns the satirist about the dangers of his trade, and 'ut' after a verb of fearing does mean 'that … not'.

1.2.3.14-f55.accuracy_reason: The anecdote is in Diogenes Laertius 6.26: Diogenes trampled Plato's carpets, and Plato replied that he did so with another kind of pride.

1.2.3.14-f61.accuracy_reason: Martial 5.8.1 opens 'Edictum domini deique nostri', using Domitian's title 'dominus et deus'.

1.2.3.14-f67.accuracy_reason: Correct: Aeneid 1.475, from the description of the scene of Troilus on the temple at Carthage.

1.2.3.14-f71.accuracy_reason: The phrase is Lucan, Pharsalia 1.93 ('omnisque potestas impatiens consortis erit'), said of power shared in the triumvirate. The note is also right that Burton's English moves on to the Juvenal allusion and does not translate this phrase.

1.2.3.14-f72.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.166–167 is the Hannibal passage ('i, demens, et saevas curre per Alpes / ut pueris placeas et declamatio fias'). 'Aude aliquid' does come from Juvenal 1.73.

1.2.3.14-f76.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Domitian 13.2, has 'Dominus et deus noster hoc fieri iubet'. The note gives Burton's changes correctly.

1.2.3.14-f77.accuracy_reason: Velleius Paterculus 2.82 describes Antony as the new Liber Pater in Alexandria. Velleius' work is in two books, so 'vol. post.' means the second.

1.2.3.14-f84.accuracy_reason: 'Dowager' together with Burton's sidenote points to Catherine of Aragon, to whom this saying (reported by Vives) is attributed.

1.2.3.14-f86.accuracy_reason: The phrase is Horace, Epistles 2.2.140, from the story of the Argive who was cured of his happy delusion and was sorry for it.
